topic: The body's fast stress response, how a work message can set it off, and pausing before replying
scope_note: Conservative, textbook-level physiology in plain words. No numbers. Wellbeing at work, not medical advice.

facts.statement: When the brain perceives a threat, the body starts a fast stress response, often called the fight or flight response, that prepares it for physical action.
facts.reference_hint: Walter Cannon's work in the early twentieth century; any physiology textbook

facts.statement: Within seconds of the alarm, the adrenal glands release adrenaline, also called epinephrine.
facts.reference_hint: Standard endocrinology; e.g. Harvard Health Publishing, Understanding the stress response

facts.statement: Adrenaline makes the heart beat faster, quickens breathing and releases stored energy into the blood, so the muscles are ready to act.
A slower hormonal chain releases cortisol, which keeps energy available for as long as the threat seems to last.
facts.caveat: Cortisol has many roles beyond stress; this is the simplified stress-related role.

facts.statement: During the response the body turns down functions that are not urgent for immediate survival, such as digestion.
facts.reference_hint: Standard physiology of the sympathetic response

facts.statement: Cortisol damps down some immune activity while the stress response continues.
facts.reference_hint: Glucocorticoid effects on immunity; standard endocrinology
facts.caveat: Short, brief stress can also briefly boost some immune responses; the effect depends on duration.

facts.statement: Acute stress narrows attention toward the perceived threat and can make careful, flexible thinking harder in the moment.
facts.reference_hint: Arnsten (2009), Nature Reviews Neuroscience, on stress and prefrontal function
facts.caveat: Effects vary with the person and how strong the stress is; mild stress can sharpen simple tasks.

facts.statement: The response evolved to help animals and people deal with short, physical dangers.
facts.reference_hint: Evolutionary account in standard stress physiology, e.g. Sapolsky, Why Zebras Don't Get Ulcers
facts.caveat: An explanatory account of origin, not something measured directly.

facts.statement: The same response can be set off by psychological pressures with no physical danger, such as deadlines, conflict or being judged by others.
facts.reference_hint: Dickerson and Kemeny (2004), Psychological Bulletin, on social-evaluative threat

facts.statement: When the perceived threat passes, the body's calming system brings heart rate and arousal back down, which takes some time rather than happening instantly.
facts.caveat: How long this takes varies; no fixed time is claimed.

facts.statement: Pausing before acting on a strong reaction gives slower, deliberate thinking a chance to take part, which can make an impulsive reply less likely.
facts.caveat: A low-risk everyday practice, not a treatment; evidence is general rather than specific to email.

facts.statement: A stress response in the moment is normal and useful; stress that keeps going and does not ease is worth talking to a doctor or a support service about.
facts.reference_hint: Public health guidance, e.g. the NHS and WHO pages on stress

not_claimed: any fixed time for how long adrenaline or cortisol last
that a breathing exercise or a pause cures anxiety
a literal 'lizard brain' or 'hijack' that takes over the mind
that the body literally cannot tell an email from a predator (say instead: the same alarm can go off)
any percentage of workers who are stressed
